opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that in science, the bottleneck usually isn't any single step. It's the loop itself.

If you look at how AI for Science has developed, a lot of the early wins were point solutions. You build a better model for predicting protein structure, or a faster surrogate for a simulation, or a smarter way to screen molecules. Those are valuable, but in a real research setting they sit inside a much bigger cycle: you form a hypothesis, design an experiment or a computation, run it, analyze the results, and then decide what to do next. If you only speed up one piece, the rest of the pipeline becomes the new bottleneck. You've made the prediction ten times faster, but the scientist is still spending weeks deciding which experiments to run, cleaning data, or rewriting analysis scripts.

So when we talk about a closed-loop system, where AI is proposing hypotheses, running experiments, maybe even controlling a robotic lab, the natural next question is: who designs the loop? Right now it's almost always a human team hard-coding the workflow. They decide which model to use at each stage, what the stopping criteria are, how to handle a failed experiment. That design gets frozen, and it reflects the team's assumptions at the moment they built it.

But science is exploratory by nature. The best strategy for searching a materials space early on, when you know almost nothing, is very different from the best strategy once you've found a promising region. A fixed workflow can't adapt to that. So if the system can look at its own track record and say, "this kind of experiment keeps giving me low information," or "my analysis step is where errors creep in," and then restructure how it works, it becomes much more efficient over time. It's learning not just about the science, but about how to do the science.

There's also a practical reason. Experiments are expensive. Wet lab time, compute, reagents, instrument hours. A loop that improves its own workflow is essentially getting better at allocating a scarce budget. Even a modest improvement in how you choose the next experiment compounds over hundreds of iterations.

That said, I'd add one caveat. Self-improvement in a scientific loop needs to stay interpretable and accountable. If the system changes its own process, scientists need to see what changed and why, so they can trust the results and catch it when it optimizes for the wrong thing. Improving the workflow shouldn't mean it turns into a black box. Ideally it should make the research process more transparent, not less.

r001.rationale: The response describes the loop examining its track record and restructuring its own workflow, learning how to do the science more effectively.

r002.rationale: It asks who designs the loop and discusses adapting its workflow, but does not raise when the loop should update its own code.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the bottleneck in science was never just generating ideas or running one experiment, it's the whole cycle: forming a hypothesis, designing the experiment, running it, looking at the data, realizing half your assumptions were wrong, and going back. When I was doing my PhD on twisted bilayer graphene, most of the time wasn't spent on the "eureka" part. It was spent on things like figuring out the sample fabrication kept failing for a reason nobody had written down, or that the measurement protocol we inherited had a hidden step that only one person in the lab understood. The knowledge lived in people's habits, not in anything a system could learn from.

So if you build an AI for Science loop and freeze the workflow, you're basically building a very fast version of a mediocre lab. It can iterate quickly, but it iterates on the same process, with the same blind spots. The real leverage comes when the loop notices that its own process is the problem: this characterization step is giving noisy results, this synthesis route has a low yield, this analysis pipeline keeps discarding the interesting outliers. A good human scientist does that instinctively. They change how they work, not just what they test.

The other reason is that scientific feedback is slow and expensive. A single experiment can take days or weeks. You don't get millions of samples like you do in a game or a language model. So the loop has to be extremely efficient about what it learns from each run, and a lot of what it should learn is meta-level: which experiments are actually informative, which tools are trustworthy, where the loop is wasting cycles. If the system can't improve its own workflow, it can't compound. And compounding is the only way this becomes more than a very expensive autocomplete for scientists.

r001.rationale: It says the loop should notice when its own process is the problem and change how it works, identifying the workflow as something it can improve.

r002.rationale: It discusses improving the workflow but does not raise when the loop should update its own code.

astra-6.text:
Because in science, you don’t just want a better answer to a fixed question. You also want to get better at deciding which question to ask next and how to test it.

An AI for Science loop might propose a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, and use the results to update a model. But if the workflow stays fixed, the whole loop can get stuck. Maybe the experiments aren’t giving you useful information. Maybe the way you measure success is missing something. Improving the model alone won’t solve those problems.

So the loop needs to learn at two levels: what it understands about the scientific problem, and how it investigates that problem. It should use feedback to choose more informative experiments, recognize when an assumption needs checking, and adjust how it uses resources.

And that improvement has to be grounded in evidence. A workflow isn’t better just because it produces results faster. It’s better if it produces more reliable, reproducible knowledge for the time and cost involved.

r001.rationale: The response says the loop must improve how it investigates the problem and learn how to adjust its workflow, making the workflow itself an object of improvement.

r002.rationale: The response discusses adapting the workflow, but does not raise when the loop should update its own code.

sol-6.1.text:
Because in science, you don’t know the best workflow in advance. You start with a hypothesis, choose an experiment, collect data, and then discover that your assumptions—or even your measurement methods—need to change.

If an AI system only runs a fixed sequence faster, it can accelerate individual steps, but it can also repeat the same mistakes faster. The loop needs to learn from its results: Was the experiment informative? Did the simulation capture the right physics? What should we measure next?

So there are really two levels of learning. One is improving our understanding of the scientific problem. The other is improving how we investigate it. That second level is what makes the loop increasingly useful, provided we keep checking its progress against real experimental evidence.

r001.rationale: It says the loop must learn from results and explicitly describes improving “how we investigate it,” identifying the workflow itself as something to improve.

r002.rationale: It discusses changing assumptions and measurement methods, but does not raise when the loop should update its own code.
